label: AQ 0001
title: The pipeline that beat the agent

questions.q: When would you choose the loop anyway?
questions.a: When the steps can't be known in advance: you have to reproduce the bug first, the change touches many files, or test failures and error messages need reading. Also when the model is strong at using tools.

teach.title: How it works: what to check when a pipeline wins

questions.q: How would you make your agent beat the pipeline?
questions.a: Add a checking step (reproduce the bug, then run the tests), improve the tools, cap the number of steps, and start the agent from the pipeline's “find the file” result instead of from scratch.

questions.q: What does the loop cost you?
questions.a: More tokens, more time and more ways to fail. Set a step limit and a spending limit, and compare cost per solved bug, not cost per run.

questions.q: In one sentence, what's the difference between a pipeline and an agent?
questions.a: In a pipeline your code fixes the steps ahead of time. In an agent the model picks each next step itself, based on what it has seen so far.

questions.q: Each step is right 90% of the time. Roughly how often does a 10-step run go fully right?
questions.a: About 35%, because 0.9 multiplied by itself 10 times is about 0.35.

questions.q: Name the three things you check before saying “loops aren't worth it”.
questions.a: The task (does it fit a fixed route?), the harness (tools and feedback) and the model (is it trained for loops?). Then compare fairly: same model, same budget.
